summary: This April 1st joke RFC specifies Scenic Routing for IPv6, a humorous scheme in the spirit of Green IT in which packets are routed to get as much fresh-air time as possible. It is not meant to be implemented.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke: it suggests that data packets should take the long way through pretty places and get lots of fresh air, like a sightseeing trip.

subtitle: A humorous IPv6 proposal to route packets through scenic wireless paths.

tldr.problem: Network packets are confined to dark fiber underground; they deserve fresh air and sunlight like any traveler.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7511 proposes Scenic Routing via a new IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option that directs routers to prefer Avian IP Carriers (pigeons) and wireless links for maximum packet enjoyment.
tldr.outcome: This is an April Fools joke and not meant to be implemented. It humorously references RFC 1149 (IP over pigeons) and satirizes Green IT concerns while maintaining strict RFC formatting.

today: RFC 7511 is an April Fools joke and is not a standard. It is widely recognized as humor and is not implemented in any production system. The RFC is valued for its creativity and for keeping the lighter side of networking alive.

sections.title: The Scenic Routing Concept
sections.content:
RFC 7511, published on April 1st, 2015, humorously proposes that network packets deserve a better life. Instead of being forced through miles of dark fiber at increasingly high speeds, packets could be routed to get as much fresh air and sunlight as possible. The proposal invokes Green IT, not by reducing energy consumption but by giving packets an outdoor experience.

The RFC cites RFC 5841 (Packet Moods) and RFC 1149 (Avian IP Carriers—using pigeons to deliver IP datagrams) as precedent, and suggests that packets using wireless links or pigeon-based delivery would be happier and more eco-conscious.
sections.plainLanguage: A joke RFC that feels sorry for data packets trapped in cables and suggests letting them travel through the air and sunshine instead.

sections.title: The Scenic Routing Option
sections.content: The proposal includes a new IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option called the Scenic Routing Option (SRO). Packets can set an 8-bit parameter field specifying the level of scenic preference (none, might, should, or must), whether to allow Avian IP Carriers, whether to allow wireless links, and which type should be preferred. Routers implementing Scenic Routing would then choose paths with the longest wireless or pigeon-based portions, even if other paths are cheaper.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets can carry a flag saying 'please route me through wireless or pigeons if you can' or 'you must'.

sections.title: Why This Matters (Humorously)
sections.content:
The RFC tongue-in-cheek explores implications for routers, hosts, and proxy servers. Routers should maintain separate scenic MPLS paths. Hosts should honor incoming scenic requests and apply them to return traffic. The RFC even suggests that scenic routing could expose packets to different cultures around the globe, promoting understanding and acceptance of cultural differences.

Of course, the RFC acknowledges serious concerns: unattended machines cannot enjoy scenery, latency increases, and the whole idea is impractical. But the humor is consistent and the RFC follows strict IETF format throughout.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke extends to routers and browsers respecting scenic preferences, and to packets broadening their cultural horizons. It's funny, but the real point is that this should never actually be implemented.

references.text: Waitzman, D., "Standard for the transmission of IP datagrams on avian carriers", RFC 1149, April 1990.
